title: Frequencies and nearest points
sub: A frequency map plus a heap of k, buckets in O(n), K Closest Points without a square root, and the k nearest enemies in Unity
cards/0/title: The problem: two stages in one
cards/0/body:
Top K Frequent Elements (LeetCode #347). Given an array nums and a number k, return the k most frequent elements in any order. Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵, |nums[i]| ≤ 10⁴, k is at most the number of distinct values, and the answer is unique — there are no ties at the edge of the top. The statement asks for something better than O(n log n).

The problem has two stages, each with its own signal:

1. “How many times” — counters: a map “value → frequency”, one pass, O(n). That is the reflex from the unit on hash maps.
2. “The k best” — the heap of k elements from the previous lesson, except the priority is the frequency, not the value itself.

From here on, m is the number of distinct values: m ≤ n, and the second stage works with m “value, frequency” pairs rather than n elements.
cards/0/code:
int[] a = TopKFrequent(new[] { 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 }, 2);   // [1, 2]: ×3 and ×2
// the map after the first stage: { 1 → 3, 2 → 2, 3 → 1 }, m = 3
cards/1/q: Which problems need both stages — counters and picking the k best? Select all.
cards/1/options/0: The 10 most frequent words in a chat log
cards/1/options/1: A match log is a list of killer ids; find the 3 players with the most kills
cards/1/options/2: The k longest words of a text
cards/1/options/3: The first non-repeating character of a string
cards/1/explain: Frequent words and top killers: first a frequency map, then the top k by frequency. Longest words need only the second stage: a length does not have to be accumulated, it is known at once, so a heap of k by length is enough. The first non-repeating character needs only the first stage: counters and a second pass over the string — there is nothing to pick the k best from.
cards/2/title: The naive solution: sort the frequencies
cards/2/body:
Count the frequencies and sort the m pairs by descending frequency: O(n + m log m). In the worst case all values are distinct, m = n = 10⁵ — about 1.7·10⁶ comparisons, so it passes time-wise. But that is exactly the O(n log n) you are asked to beat: the whole map gets sorted, while you need k pairs.

The LINQ version is short, and in an interview you can name it as the baseline. The cost: OrderByDescending copies all m pairs into a buffer, plus iterator objects and the result array — in hot Unity code that is garbage for the GC on every call. In modern .NET the chain OrderBy(…).Take(k) internally orders only the first k (a partial quicksort), but that is an implementation detail: in an interview reason about O(m log m), and the buffer of m pairs is allocated anyway.

GetValueOrDefault is a dictionary extension from .NET Core 2.0 and .NET Standard 2.1, available in Unity: for a new key it returns 0, whereas the indexer count[x] would throw KeyNotFoundException.
cards/3/title: The idea: a min-heap of k by frequency
cards/3/body:
The second stage is the same “top k” as in the previous lesson. Walk over the map’s pairs and enqueue the value with the frequency as priority: Enqueue(x, f). If the heap now holds k + 1 pairs, Dequeue removes the rarest one.

Invariant: the heap holds the k most frequent of the pairs seen so far, and the root is the rarest of them, the entry threshold.

Cost: O(n) for the map and O(m log k) for the heap — O(n + m log k), memory O(m + k). With k = 10 and m = 10⁵ the heap is about 3.3·10⁵ steps against 1.7·10⁶ for sorting.

Answer order. Dequeue yields pairs from the rarest to the most frequent, so the array is filled from the end — the most frequent ends up first. The statement allows any order, but interviewers often ask “and in descending order?” — that is your answer.

Ties. PriorityQueue is not stable (the lesson on .NET collections): of two pairs with the same frequency either may be thrown out. Here that is safe — the statement promises no ties at the edge of the top. Without that promise, agree on how ties are broken and put it into the priority: (frequency, value).
cards/4/q: Assemble the solution: a frequency map and a min-heap of k.
cards/4/explain: For a new key the indexer count[x] throws KeyNotFoundException, while GetValueOrDefault returns 0. The priority is the frequency f: then the rarest pair sits at the root, and that is the one to remove. With priority x the heap would select by value, and with −f it would throw out the most frequent. Fill the array from the last index k − 1: the rarest of the k comes out first, the most frequent comes out last and lands in res[0]. With i = k the code would run past the end of the array.
cards/5/task: Step through the trace on [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 5], k = 2. The frequencies are already counted; the rig asks twice whom Dequeue will remove. Watch the frequency at the root.
cards/5/goal/asks/0/q: 4 (×4) has arrived. The heap holds 2 (×2), 1 (×3), 4 (×4) — size 3 > k. Whom will Dequeue remove?
cards/5/goal/asks/0/explain: The priority is the frequency, and the root of a min-heap holds the smallest: ×2. So 2 leaves, and 1 (×3) and 4 (×4) remain. The new threshold is ×3: from now on only a value seen more than three times gets into the top.
cards/5/goal/asks/1/q: 5 (×1) has arrived and risen to the root: 5 (×1), 4 (×4), 1 (×3). Whom will Dequeue remove?
cards/5/goal/asks/1/explain: The 5 is rarer than the threshold ×3 — it entered the heap and left right away. That is the same wasted sift up and sift down as in the previous lesson; EnqueueDequeue would have returned it without any work. The result is 1 and 4, the most frequent.
cards/6/body:
The frequency of any value is an integer from 1 to n. So instead of comparing by frequency you can distribute: an array buckets of length n + 1, where buckets[f] holds the values that occurred exactly f times. Then walk from f = n downwards and collect until you have k.

This is counting sort by frequency: the keys are small integers in a known range, and no comparisons are needed. Time is O(n): the map takes n, distributing takes m, the walk takes n + 1 buckets. Memory is O(n): the bucket array plus the lists.

When buckets lose to a heap. The bucket array has length n + 1 however many distinct values there are. If n is huge and m is small — 10⁸ events and 1000 distinct ids — buckets allocate 10⁸ references (800 MB on 64 bits), while the heap needs m log k ≈ 3300 steps and O(k) memory. Buckets are good when n is moderate and you want a true O(n). You can use length maxFreq + 1 instead of n + 1, but in the worst case it is the same thing.
cards/6/deep:
Quickselect on frequencies. Another O(m) on average: write the m distinct values into an array and run the quickselect from the previous lesson, comparing by frequency; the k most frequent end up on one side of position m − k. The worst case is O(m²) and the input gets rearranged, but you do not need a bucket array of length n.

SortedSet as a heap with removal. If the top keeps changing — frequencies go up and down, like a counter of popular items in a game store — a heap lacks priority updates. SortedSet<T> can Remove in O(log n), and Min and Max walk down to the extreme node, also O(log n). Updating a frequency means removing the old pair and inserting the new one.

The trap: equal elements collapse. A set treats elements with CompareTo == 0 as the same. A SortedSet<int> with a “by frequency” comparer returns false from Add on a second value with the same frequency — and the value silently disappears. The key is the pair (frequency, value): a tuple compares field by field, and no two pairs are equal as long as the values are unique. For elements without a natural unique field you add an id or an insertion number.

Ties by rule. In Top K Frequent Words (#692), among equal frequencies the word that comes first alphabetically ranks higher. For a min-heap of k that is the comparer “frequency ascending, then word descending”: the worst candidate must sit at the root, and the worst among equals is the one later in the alphabet. Compare strings with string.CompareOrdinal: the statement has only lowercase Latin letters, and culture-aware comparison is unnecessary here.
cards/7/q: A server log holds 10⁸ events with 1000 distinct player ids. You need the 10 most active players. The frequency map is ready — what do you use for the second stage?
cards/7/options/0: A heap of 10 by frequency: m log k ≈ 3300 steps, O(k) memory
cards/7/options/1: Buckets: O(n) is always better than O(m log k)
cards/7/options/2: Sort the 1000 pairs by frequency and take 10 — that is the same as buckets
cards/7/explain: The second stage works with m = 1000 pairs. The heap takes 1000 · log₂ 10 ≈ 3300 steps. Buckets set up an array of length n + 1 = 10⁸ + 1 — 800 MB of references for a thousand values. Sorting 1000 pairs is about 10⁴ comparisons, also instant, but that is neither buckets nor O(n).
cards/7/wrong/1: The O(n) of buckets is a walk over n + 1 buckets and the memory for them. With n = 10⁸ and m = 1000, a heap over m pairs is orders of magnitude cheaper.
cards/7/wrong/2: Sorting 1000 pairs is O(m log m), about 10⁴ comparisons: it works, but buckets distribute without comparisons and need an array of length n + 1. They are different techniques with different costs.
cards/8/title: K Closest Points: distance without a square root
cards/8/body:
K Closest Points to Origin (LeetCode #973). Given points points[i] = [x, y] and a number k, return the k points closest to the origin, in any order. Constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 10⁴, |x|, |y| ≤ 10⁴.

No square root needed. The distance is √(x² + y²), and the square root is monotonic: if a² < b², then a < b. Compare squares — no Math.Sqrt and no double. The square is at most 2·10⁸, and int.MaxValue ≈ 2.1·10⁹ — it fits. With coordinates up to 10⁵ it no longer fits: 2·10¹⁰, so compute in long.

The heap mirrors the previous lesson. You need the k smallest distances, so you must throw out the farthest candidate: a max-heap by distance of k elements. The root is the farthest of the k closest, the entry threshold. O(n log k), memory O(k). The rule: for the k smallest use a max-heap, for the k largest a min-heap; the root always holds whoever gets thrown out first. In Unity, use the MinHeap<T> from the previous lesson with the same descending comparer.

Quickselect by distance also works — O(n) on average, at the same price: the input is rearranged and it does not work on a stream.
cards/9/q: This code returns the k farthest points instead of the closest. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/9/explain: The default queue is a min-heap: the closest point sits at the root, and Dequeue throws exactly that one out every time. The heap is left with the k farthest. You need a max-heap: a descending comparer or priority −d (the square is at most 2·10⁸, so negation is safe).
cards/10/body:
A tower needs the k nearest enemies, an AI needs the k nearest pieces of cover. This is #973 in a game, with adjustments for the engine.

sqrMagnitude, not Distance. Vector3.Distance and magnitude take a square root; (a − b).sqrMagnitude does not, and the order is the same. Compare a radius squared too: d < r * r.

Small k — a buffer instead of a heap. For k up to 10–20, keep a sorted array of k: a new enemy is first compared with the worst of the best — almost always a rejection after one comparison — and if it passes, it is put in place by insertion. Worst case O(n·k), in practice O(n) with a tiny constant, and not a single allocation: the buffers are fields, and foreach over a List<T> uses a struct enumerator.

Positions. transform.position is a call into the native side of the engine, not a field read. With thousands of objects, keep positions in your own array and update them once per frame.

When you need a grid. One tower and 200 enemies — a plain pass, 200 comparisons. But if 1000 units look for neighbours every frame, the “everyone with everyone” pass is 10⁶ distances per frame. As a rough estimate that is a few milliseconds, more on a mobile CPU — a noticeable share of the 16 ms budget, and it grows quadratically: 3000 units already means 9·10⁶. Then you need a spatial grid or hash: candidates come only from neighbouring cells, and inside them the same buffer of k. Details are in the unit on pathfinding and space. If the enemies have colliders, Physics.OverlapSphereNonAlloc also gives you the candidates within a radius.
cards/11/q: Unity: 1000 units, and every frame each one needs its 5 nearest neighbours to avoid collisions. What do you do?
cards/11/options/0: A spatial grid: candidates only from neighbouring cells, and inside them a buffer of 5
cards/11/options/1: For each unit, a pass over all the others with a buffer of 5: that is O(n) per unit, linear
cards/11/options/2: For each unit, a min-heap of all 1000 by distance and Dequeue 5 times
cards/11/explain: A pass over everyone is O(n) per unit, but there are n units: 10⁶ distances per frame — a few milliseconds of a 16 ms budget, more on mobile, and the growth is quadratic. A grid leaves each unit a few dozen candidates from neighbouring cells, and the same buffer picks the five. This is now a question of spatial partitioning, not of heaps.
cards/11/wrong/1: O(n) is per unit. For all of them it is n², 10⁶ distances per frame: a few milliseconds out of 16, and four times more every time the number of units doubles.
cards/11/wrong/2: A heap of all 1000 is the same quadratic work, plus n log n for the insertions. And k = 5 already makes a buffer cheaper than a heap.
cards/12/q: You are solving Top K Frequent Elements out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: the answer order, whether there are ties at the edge of the top, what are n and k
cards/12/items/1: Name the two stages: a frequency map in O(n), then picking the k best
cards/12/items/2: Baseline: sort the m pairs by frequency — O(n + m log m)
cards/12/items/3: Idea: a min-heap of k by frequency, the root is the rarest of the best
cards/12/items/4: Write the code and run [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], k = 2
cards/12/items/5: Complexity: O(n + m log k) time, O(m + k) memory
cards/12/items/6: If asked for O(n): buckets by frequency — and say when they lose to a heap
cards/12/explain: The question about ties decides whether you need a composite priority. Naming the two stages up front shows that the problem breaks into familiar parts. Buckets answer “and in O(n)?”, together with their price: an array of length n + 1.
